full_text: Pre-commit hooks. Running checks before committing changes in software development. Ensuring code quality and consistency is crucial. One effective way to achieve this is by using pre-commit hooks. These hooks are automated checks that run before you commit your code, helping you catch issues early and maintain a high standard of code quality. What are pre-commit hooks? Pre-commit hooks are scripts that run automatically before a commit is completed in Git. They allow you to inspect the changes that are about to be committed and can prevent the commit if certain conditions aren't met. The purpose of pre-commit hooks are to catch issues early in development, enforce code quality standards, prevent problematic code from entering the repository, automate repetitive checks, and maintain consistency across team members. How do pre-commit hooks work? First, a developer adds files to the staging area with the command git add. Then, a developer runs git commit to save changes, initiating the commit process. Pre-commit hooks then run automatically to check the code. Finally, the commit proceeds or is blocked based on the hook results. This ensures that only code that meets the defined standards is committed to the repository. Here are some common use cases for pre-commit hooks. Code linting enforces coding style and catches syntax errors using tools like ESLint, Pyint or Rubocop. Unit testing runs tests to ensure code changes don't break existing functionality. Code formatting automatically formats code using tools like prettier, black, or god. Security scanning checks for security vulnerabilities, secrets or credentials in code. Code complexity analyzes and limits code complexity to maintain maintainability. Finally, pre-commit hooks can prevent commits to protected branches or with specific patterns like to-do comments. Let's discuss setting up pre-commit hooks. For manual setup, first create agit/hooks directory in your repository. Next, create a file named pre-commit with no extension. Then make the file executable with the command schmod plus x. Write your script using bash, python, or any executable language. Finally, test your hook by making a commit. Here's a basic pre-commit hook example. The script starts with a shebang line specifying that it should be executed with bash. It then echoes which means prints running pre-commit hook. The script checks for console.log statements in JavaScript files, uses git diff to find change files and then uses gp to search for console.log statements. If console.log is found, it prints an error message and exits with code one which indicates failure. Otherwise, it exits with code zero indicating success. An easier way to set up pre-commit hooks is by using the pre-commit framework. The pre-commit framework is a Python package that simplifies managing and maintaining pre-commit hooks. It provides a collection of readytouse hooks and makes it easy to share hooks across projects. To use it, first install pre-commit using the command pip install pre-commit. Next, create a file named pre-commit config.yaml. Then install hooks by running the command pre-commit install. Finally, commit changes as usual. Here's a sample configuration file. Under repos, it specifies three repositories. Pre-commit/precommit hooks, psf/black, and pick a/flake 8. For each repository, it defines a set of hooks to run such as trailing whites space, end of file fixer, check yaml, black, and flake 8. Let's see how to create custom pre-commit hooks. When built-in hooks don't meet your needs, you can create custom hooks tailored to your project requirements. First, script should be executable and have a shebang line. Next, return exit code zero for success. non-zero for failure. Keep hooks focused on a single responsibility. Include clear error messages for failures. Test hooks thoroughly before deployment. And finally, document hook behavior for team members. Here's how to use a custom hook in the pre-commit framework. Here, a local repository is defined and a hook named forbidden words is set up to check for forbidden words like to-do or fem. The hook is implemented in the file check_forbidden_words py uses Python and applies to text files excluding files in the.getit directory. This configuration ensures that the custom hook runs during the commit stage. Here are some best practices for pre-commit hooks. Keep hooks fast. So optimize hooks for speed to avoid disrupting workflow. Run comprehensive tests in continuous integration and continuous delivery pipelines instead of pre-commit hooks. Use version control for your hooks, storing hook configurations in version control to ensure consistency across all team members and environments. Focus on specific issues. Design hooks to catch specific problems rather than trying to solve everything. Each hook should have a clear single responsibility. Finally, provide bypass options. Allow developers to bypass hooks in exceptional cases using the command git commit double- no-verify, but log these exceptions. In summary, pre-commit hooks automate code quality checks before changes are committed. They help catch issues early in the development process. They can be set up manually or using frameworks like pre-commit. Pre-commit hooks enforce consistent standards across team members. For further resources, you can visit precommit.com, gsecm.com/doccks/gith hooks, and github.com/precommit/precommit hooks. If you like this video, hit that like button and don't forget to subscribe.
